title: How universities can lead the way towards a sustainable future
desc:
Join the launch of our Sustainable Imperial Strategy (2026–2031) .

As a community of thinkers, teachers, professionals and innovators – how do we best translat e our sustainability ideas into real work i mpact? How do we bring our ingenuity to guide our institution and the world beyond to a more sustainable future?

Whether you are deeply involved in sustainability or just starting out, you are a vital part of our collective journey towards a more sustainable Imperial and planet.

Across a short presentation, an exhibition showcase, and networking afternoon tea, you’ll meet the staff, students, alumni and community members bringing our sustainability ambitions to reality – and learn how you can get involved.

Join us as we unveil our vision for the next five years and beyond.

title: Deep Learning Models with Hard Physical and Logical Constraints
desc:
Title: Deep Learning Models with Hard Physical and Logical Constraints

Abstract: Modern deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in computer vision, natural language processing, and a growing range of scientific applications, from image analysis to molecular and materials modeling. However, their direct application to chemical engineering problems remains challenging because engineering systems are governed by strict physical and logical constraints and are often characterized by sparse, expensive data.

Standard neural networks may produce accurate predictions on average, yet still violate fundamental principles such as mass and energy balances, operational limits, or logical rules, making them unreliable for scientific and industrial use. In this talk, I will present a…
venue: LT2, ACE Extension, South Kensington Campus

title: GATP Seminar — Eric Yen-Yo Chen (EPFL): Langlands functoriality of Hitchin systems
desc:
Traditionally, Langlands functoriality refers to the identification of automorphic forms whose parameters take a special shape. In this talk, we explain how to ask analogous questions on the Hitchin moduli space using perspectives from the relative Langlands program. We gain, in this setting, the advantage of working with a version of Langlands duality which is readily computable, and if time permits we will discuss the ramifications of these calculations for automorphic periods and L-functions.

This will be a Zoom talk we will watch together in Huxley 411, or you can use the zoom link (available upon request).
venue: Huxley 411, Huxley Building, South Kensington Campus

title: SPC Seminar – Climate – Alexey Fedorov (Yale)
desc:
Speaker: Alexey Federov (Yale)

Title: El Nino and global warming: from multi-year prediction to climate change projections

Abstract: The response of the tropical Pacific mean state and the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) to rising atmospheric CO₂ concentrations remains highly uncertain. For example, the projected development of enhanced warming in the eastern equatorial Pacific, along with the associated weakening of the Walker circulation, contrasts with the strengthening of the Walker circulation observed over the past 30–40 years. Here, I discuss the key mechanisms shaping ongoing and future changes in the tropical Pacific across different timescales, as well as the projected strengthening of ENSO across a wide range of realistic and idealized global warming experiments and…

title: SPC Seminar – Climate – Harri Kokkola (FMI)
desc:
Speaker : Harri Kokkola (FMI)

Title : Combining numerical modelling and observations in determining aerosol-cloud interactions

Abstract : This presentation examines how aerosol–cloud interactions can be distinguished from natural cloud variability, combining observational, modelling, and satellite approaches developed at the Atmospheric Research Centre of Eastern Finland. A key focus is on large-eddy simulations to study aerosol effects and their influence on precipitation, emphasizing the challenges in quantifying how changes in aerosol load affects the amount of precipitation. The presentation also addresses biases in satellite-derived aerosol–cloud interaction metrics, showing how retrieval errors and cloud variability can distort observed relationships. title: Mechanical Engineering 3rd Year ‘Design Make and Test’ Exhibition
desc:
The Design Make and Test project is a major part of the Mechanical Engineering curriculum, and is a year-long engineering design project carried out by groups of third year students in the Department of Mechanical Engineering.

The groups run their project as a small engineering consultancy. Students are given a brief for a sub-assembly of a larger project and must develop ideas, develop concepts, then build and test a final prototype product. Further to this, each sub-assembly must be compatible with the other sub-assemblies in that project.

The final task during the year is to present this project at the DMT exhibition, which this year will be taking place between 16.00 and 18.00 on Tuesday 9 June, in the College Main Entrance and the CAGB Foyer. All are welcome to come and see what…

title: London Heilbronn Colloquium: Federico Ardila (QMUL)
desc:
Federico Ardila (QMUL): Geometry, Robots and Society

Abstract: How do we move a robot quickly from one position to another? To answer this question, we need to understand its configuration space, a “map” where we can find every possible position of the robot. Unfortunately, these spaces are very large, they live in very high-dimensions, and they are very difficult to visualize. Fortunately, geometric group theorists and combinatorialists have encountered and studied similar spaces before. Thanks to the tools they’ve developed, we can build “remote controls” to navigate these complicated spaces; this allows us to move (some) robots optimally. As the imaginary border between “pure” and “applied” mathematics disappears before our eyes, we face an important ethical question that we cannot…
